teaser.text: Imperial Brands is a tobacco and nicotine company: it sells products that adults buy repeatedly, through shops and other businesses. To understand its business, follow a product from leaf or ingredients to a packet, pouch or device, then follow the money back through the supply chain.

blocks.heading: Where could Imperial's shares be in October 2027 and October 2029?

paragraphs.text: The bear case requires legal cigarette volumes and market share to weaken faster than pricing can compensate, especially in Australia, while NGP remains loss-making. Legal and transformation cash costs then constrain distributions, buybacks disappoint and debt stays elevated. The bear path gives 2563.63 GBp in October 2027 and 2069.16 GBp in October 2029. Its 30% probability reflects credible downside, but the need for several pressures to persist despite Imperial’s record of rising adjusted earnings.

The bull case requires stronger share retention, timely transformation savings and NGP progress toward profitability. Better cash generation funds investment and buybacks without stretching leverage, while investors reward a more durable earnings outlook. The bull path gives 3750.35 GBp in October 2027 and 6030.56 GBp in October 2029. Its 20% probability reflects substantial upside, but several unproven improvements must arrive together.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for Imperial?

paragraphs.text: Base earnings start at £2,576m, close to FY2025 adjusted net income of £2,598m. They rise to £2,624m in the next window and £2,673m in the last. Revenue is broadly stable, beginning at £32,200m and ending at £32,600m. Margin moves from 8.0% to 8.2%, near FY2025’s roughly 8.1%, because guidance allows modest operating gains but interest and tax offset some benefit. Bear earnings fall to £2,424m and then £2,261m. They reach £2,101m in the last window as volume, illicit-market and NGP pressures compress revenue and margin. Bull earnings rise to £2,689m and £2,838m before reaching £2,990m, as pricing holds, savings arrive and NGP losses narrow.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay today for Imperial?

paragraphs.text: The P/E compares the share price with earnings, but trailing and forward earnings are not interchangeable. Reported earnings follow accounting rules; adjusted earnings remove items management considers unusual. The Delaware case produced a £312m accounting charge, while Imperial paid £150m in cash during the first half of FY26.

dividend.title: Imperial dividend
dividend.meta_description: Imperial pays a dividend from substantial cash generation, while dividends and buybacks can exceed free cash flow.
dividend.opening: In FY2025, Imperial paid £1,558 million in dividends, against £2,692 million of free cash flow. That cash came after capital spending, leases and interest, but dividends and buybacks together exceeded free cash flow in the latest year.
dividend.closing: The full memo also explains Imperial’s business, its rivals, its management, and its risks.

blocks.heading: How much does Imperial pay shareholders over time?

paragraphs.text: Imperial’s dividend history explains why the policy is not automatic. It cut the dividend by one-third in 2020 to accelerate debt reduction, then began buybacks in 2022. In October 2026, after completing its latest programme, Imperial announced a £1.5 billion buyback for the following year. Debt reduction created room for these distributions, but every pound returned competes with transformation, acquisitions and legal obligations.

blocks.heading: Does Imperial cover its dividend with cash?

paragraphs.text: Cash from operations was £3,627 million in FY2025. After capital spending, leases and interest, free cash flow was £2,692 million. Imperial’s own free-cash-flow measure was £2,749 million because it uses different definitions for capital spending, interest and minority dividends.

Cash did not reduce debt because distributions exceeded company-defined free cash flow. Imperial paid £1,558 million in dividends and spent £1,235 million buying back shares. Strong cash generation can therefore coexist with borrowing that stays high or rises.

By 2025, dividends and buybacks together exceeded that year’s free cash flow. Borrowing helped bridge the gap, although much new debt replaced maturing debt rather than creating entirely new spending capacity. Net debt fell across the five-year period but rose in the latest year, and Imperial’s own debt measure differs from the measure used in the table.

paragraphs.text: Imperial’s plan works only if cigarettes keep funding investment until newer nicotine products generate their own profit and cash. Capital allocation means deciding how to divide cash among investment, debt, dividends and buybacks. Imperial’s stated order is to invest first, maintain an efficient balance sheet, pay a progressive dividend and return surplus capital.

blocks.heading: What has Imperial guided for FY2026?

paragraphs.text: Imperial’s share could reach 3,063.61p in October 2027 and 3,874.76p by October 2029 if pricing, cash generation and transition execution sustain the earnings base. Management reaffirmed 3%–5% constant-currency adjusted operating-profit growth for FY2026, with low-single-digit tobacco net-revenue growth, double-digit NGP growth, high-single-digit adjusted EPS growth and more than £2,200 million of free cash flow.

blocks.heading: Has Imperial kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: The consensus predates the October reaffirmation and the FY2027 buyback announcement, so it is a dated snapshot rather than a complete picture of current expectations. Imperial has also produced two small recent full-year beats: FY2024 operating-profit growth was 4.6% against 4.3% expected, while FY2025 operating profit was about £3.99bn against £3.98bn expected.

blocks.heading: What has Imperial's revenue and profit trend been?

paragraphs.text: In the six months to March 2026, revenue rose 0.8%, but operating income fell 36.5%. Net income fell 41.2%, and diluted EPS fell 38.1%. The decline directs attention below gross profit, toward legal costs, restructuring, financing and tax.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Imperial's next results?

paragraphs.text: Imperial reports the year ended September on 17 November 2026. Investors should begin with second-half profit and earnings, then follow the cash reconciliation. The accounts will show whether trading improved as management expected and how restructuring, legal payments and shareholder returns changed debt.

July 2027 will test the Langenhagen exit, while FY2027 and FY2028 will test whether transformation spending produces the promised efficiencies. The real measure is the movement from announcement, to accounting cost, to cash payment, to completed saving.
